clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant reticulate pigmentary genodermatosis caused by heterozygous loss-of-function variants in ADAM10.
Presents in the first or second decade with slightly depressed (atrophic) hyperpigmented macules in a net-like reticulate pattern on the dorsa of the hands and feet.
Interruption or breaks of the epidermal ridge pattern (dermatoglyphics) on the palms and soles, often with palmar pits, is a characteristic sign.
Pigmentation is initially acral but may extend proximally to the limbs and trunk with age, and lesions may darken with sun exposure.
Considered part of a clinical and mechanistic spectrum with Dowling-Degos disease, and some patients display features of both.
Histology shows epidermal atrophy with elongated rete ridges and increased basal-layer melanin, without melanocyte proliferation.
The condition is purely cutaneous, with no systemic, ocular, or neurological involvement, which helps separate it from X-linked reticulate pigmentary disorder.
Reported most often in Japanese populations but described worldwide.
reference.pathophysiology: Reticulate acropigmentation of Kitamura is an autosomal dominant disorder of pigmentation caused by heterozygous loss-of-function variants in ADAM10, which encodes a disintegrin and metalloproteinase that acts as a cell-surface sheddase cleaving the ectodomains of numerous substrates, including Notch receptors and cadherins. ADAM10 contributes to keratinocyte adhesion and to the migration, dendricity, and function of melanocytes, so reduced ADAM10 activity is thought to disturb melanocyte-keratinocyte signalling and melanosome distribution, producing the characteristic reticulate deposition of melanin in the basal epidermis. Histologically there is thinning of the epidermis with elongation of the rete ridges and increased basal melanin but no increase in melanocyte number, and the disturbance of epidermal architecture underlies the breaks seen in the dermatoglyphic ridge pattern. ADAM10 lies within the same Notch-related pathway as keratin 5 (KRT5) and the glycosyltransferase and gamma-secretase genes (POFUT1, POGLUT1, PSENEN) implicated in Dowling-Degos disease, which explains the clinical and mechanistic overlap between the two conditions.
additionalDifferentials: Dowling-Degos disease (flexural reticulate hyperpigmentation with comedo-like lesions and pitted scars).
Dyschromatosis symmetrica hereditaria (acropigmentation of Dohi) with mixed hyper- and hypopigmented macules on the dorsa of the hands and feet, due to ADAR1.
Dyschromatosis universalis hereditaria with generalised mottled hyper- and hypopigmentation.
Haber syndrome (rosacea-like facial eruption with reticulate pigmentation).
Naegeli-Franceschetti-Jadassohn syndrome and dermatopathia pigmentosa reticularis (KRT14) with reticulate pigmentation, absent dermatoglyphics, hypohidrosis, and dental or nail changes.
Acquired reticulate pigmentation from arsenic exposure or post-inflammatory change.
X-linked reticulate pigmentary disorder (POLA1), which adds systemic features.
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy with histopathology of a representative macule showing epidermal atrophy, elongated rete ridges, and basal hypermelanosis.
Dermoscopy of acral lesions and inspection of palmar dermatoglyphics for ridge interruption and pits.
Molecular genetic testing for ADAM10 variants.
Detailed family history and examination of relatives given autosomal dominant inheritance.
Examination of flexural sites to assess for overlap with Dowling-Degos disease.
Wood's lamp examination to delineate the extent of epidermal pigmentation.
Systemic and ocular review to exclude features suggesting an alternative reticulate disorder.
redFlags: Systemic features such as recurrent infections, chronic diarrhoea, or keratitis with photophobia suggest X-linked reticulate pigmentary disorder rather than Kitamura disease and warrant reappraisal.
Rapid change, ulceration, or nodularity within a pigmented lesion should prompt biopsy to exclude malignancy.
Onset in adulthood or a strikingly asymmetric distribution should raise suspicion of an acquired or exogenous cause such as arsenical pigmentation.
Associated hypohidrosis, nail dystrophy, or dental anomalies point towards an ectodermal dysplasia-type reticulate disorder.
reference.prognosis: Reticulate acropigmentation of Kitamura is a benign, slowly progressive condition with no systemic consequences; pigmentation tends to increase and extend over years but represents only a cosmetic concern, and life expectancy is normal.
pitfalls: Mislabelling the condition as ordinary post-inflammatory or sun-induced pigmentation and missing the diagnostic breaks in palmar dermatoglyphics.
Failing to recognise overlap with Dowling-Degos disease, leading to incomplete counselling about the pigmentary spectrum.
Attributing systemic symptoms to Kitamura disease, which is purely cutaneous, so such features indicate a different diagnosis.
Expecting depigmenting therapies to be curative, when response is limited and the disorder is progressive.
management: Reassure that this is a benign, cosmetic condition with normal life expectancy and no systemic consequences
Advise photoprotection with sunscreen and sun avoidance, since lesions darken with ultraviolet exposure
Offer cosmetic camouflage and discuss topical agents such as retinoids or hydroquinone or laser therapy, noting their limited and variable benefit
Confirm the diagnosis where needed with skin biopsy and ADAM10 molecular testing, and assess for overlap with Dowling-Degos disease
Provide genetic counselling and examine relatives given autosomal dominant inheritance
Refer to dermatology for diagnosis and management of cosmetic concerns
